correctness.rationale: The weighted scalar p-mean has a unique root because the real p-energy is strictly convex, and implicit differentiation at nonzero residuals yields a positive sensitivity g_i=v_i|r_i|^{p-2}/sum(v_j g_j). For p>2, write the signed p-1 residual moments as two probability vectors; the dual test with d_i=(y_i-Cv_i)v_i^{q-1} has d_i+d_j<=0 on every pair and at most one positive entry, so concavity of the power sigma=(p-2)/(p-1) bounds each sign group and yields the pair maximum. Opposite-sign residuals on the winning pair realize its derivative; at other coordinates g=0. For 1<p<2, ||g||_q<=sum g and sum v_i g_i>=min(v_i) sum g give V/min(v_i); monotone smooth regularization of the p-mean passes the global bound through zero residuals. For k>=3, a balanced residual with one minimum-weight coordinate tending to zero has g_i diverge and realizes the bound. k=1 is a coordinate retraction, k=2 is an exact linear weighted mean, p=2 is orthogonal. Pair norm >=1 by retraction and Hölder equality forces equal weights for two active coordinates away from p=2. Independent constrained-residual gradient tests checked 3840 finite cases, supporting but not replacing the dual/sign and smoothing arguments.
residual_risks: The global Lipschitz supremum need not be realized by a separated pair; witnesses may be infinitesimal.
Complex scalar or nonatomic Lp cases are outside the proof; no extension inferred.
